title: Sharks: 400 million years of ocean survivors

transcriptLines.text: What if I told you there's an animal that has been around longer than trees? Stick around, because today we're diving into sharks.
Hey everyone, welcome back to the channel. If you're new here, we make short science videos about the natural world.
Sharks first appeared in the oceans more than four hundred million years ago, long before the dinosaurs.
Today there are more than five hundred species, from the tiny dwarf lanternshark to the enormous whale shark.
Unlike most fish, a shark's skeleton is not made of bone. It is made of cartilage, the same bendy material in your nose and ears.
Cartilage is lighter than bone, which helps a shark stay up in the water and turn quickly.
Most fish have a gas-filled swim bladder that helps them float, but sharks do not have one.
Instead, a shark has a huge liver filled with oil. Oil is lighter than water, so the liver works like a built-in float.
In some sharks the liver makes up a quarter of the whole body weight.
Even so, many sharks would slowly sink if they stopped swimming, so they keep moving.
Let's talk about breathing. Sharks breathe with gills, the slits you can see on the sides of the head.
As water flows over the gills, tiny blood vessels pull oxygen out of the water and into the blood.
Some sharks, like the great white, have to swim forward to push water over their gills. This is called ram ventilation.
Others, like the nurse shark, can rest on the sea floor and pump water over their gills with their mouth.
Now, the skin. If you stroked a shark from tail to head, it would feel like sandpaper.
That's because the skin is covered in tiny tooth-like scales called dermal denticles.
The denticles make little swirls in the water that cut drag, so the shark slips through the water more easily.
Engineers have even copied denticles to design faster swimsuits and smoother ship hulls.
This video is sponsored by OceanBox, the monthly subscription that sends you a new ocean science kit every month.
Each kit comes with experiments and a fun guide. Use code SHARKS for twenty percent off your first box.
OK, back to sharks. Let's talk about teeth, the part everyone wants to hear about.
Shark teeth are not fixed in the jaw like ours. They sit in rows, like a conveyor belt.
When a front tooth breaks or falls out, a tooth from the row behind moves forward to replace it.
A single shark can lose and replace tens of thousands of teeth in its lifetime.
The shape of the teeth matches the diet. Great whites have jagged, triangular teeth for slicing.
Shortfin makos have long, thin teeth for gripping slippery fish, and whale sharks barely use their tiny teeth at all.
Speaking of whale sharks, they are filter feeders. They swim with their mouth open and strain plankton out of the water.
Now for the senses. Sharks can smell blood in the water from hundreds of meters away.
Each nostril is used only for smelling, not breathing, and the shark can tell which side a scent is stronger on.
That helps it steer toward the source of a smell.
Sharks also have a line of sensors along each side of the body called the lateral line.
The lateral line feels tiny movements and pressure changes in the water, like the splashing of an injured fish.
But the most amazing sense is one we don't have at all.
Around a shark's snout are small pores filled with jelly. These are the ampullae of Lorenzini.
They detect the weak electric fields that every living animal gives off when its muscles move.
A hammerhead can find a stingray buried under the sand just by sensing its electric field.
The wide head of the hammerhead spreads these sensors out, like sweeping a metal detector over a beach.
Let's talk about how sharks have babies. Different sharks do it in very different ways.
Some sharks lay eggs in tough cases. You may have found one on a beach, it's often called a mermaid's purse.
Other sharks keep the eggs inside the body until the pups hatch, and then give birth to live young.
Baby sharks are called pups, and they are on their own from the moment they are born.
Sharks grow slowly and have few pups, which makes it hard for their numbers to recover when too many are caught.
And that's a big problem. Every year people catch tens of millions of sharks.
Many are caught by accident in nets meant for other fish, and many are hunted for their fins.
Sharks are top predators, so when they disappear, the whole food web below them can fall out of balance.
For example, without sharks, some fish that eat seagrass and coral grazers can grow out of control.
Marine protected areas, where fishing is limited, give shark populations a chance to recover.
So next time you see a shark in a movie, remember it's an ancient survivor with senses we can barely imagine.
If you enjoyed this video, hit like and subscribe so you don't miss the next one.
Thanks for watching, and see you next time.
